Use the funder’s headings in the exact order below. **Put the executive summary in the separate Cover Letter** unless the instructions explicitly allow an unheaded overview in the Project Narrative. That keeps the narrative focused on scored material and avoids adding a heading the funder didn’t request.

## Cover Letter — 1 page, separate

**Target: 275–325 words total, including the 200-word summary.** Open with the opportunity name, project title, and request amount. Use the summary below as the body, then close with the applicant’s contact information and authorized signature, if required. Don’t add a second overview that repeats the summary.

**Opening hook:** “On behalf of [Organization], I am submitting [Project Name] for consideration under [Funding Opportunity] and requesting $[amount] for [grant period].”

## Project Narrative — 8 single-spaced pages

**Working target: 3,450 words.** This is a drafting budget, not a guarantee of page fit. Check the funder’s font, margins, and spacing rules early, and leave room for headings and any tables included in the narrative. The separately uploaded budget table is outside this word budget; the **Budget Narrative** is inside it.

| Required heading | Target words | Rubric criteria addressed |
|---|---:|---|
| Need | 850 | **Need/Community Impact (30%)** — clarity of problem, target population, data |
| Approach | 1,000 | **Program Design & Activities (30%)** — program logic, timeline, staffing |
| Goals & Objectives | 425 | **Outcomes & Evaluation (20%)** — measurable outcomes, baselines, targets |
| Evaluation | 475 | **Outcomes & Evaluation (20%)** — methods, baseline collection, measurement |
| Sustainability | 150 | **Organizational Capacity & Sustainability (5%)** — continuation plans |
| Organizational Information | 150 | **Organizational Capacity & Sustainability (5%)** — relevant experience |
| Budget Narrative | 400 | **Budget & Cost Effectiveness (15%)** — clear costs, justification, value |
| **Total** | **3,450** | |

*Where two sections share a rubric category, the percentage applies to the category as a whole, not to each section.*

### Need — 850 words
**Include:** Define the problem, geography, and priority population up front. Use two or three dated sources to establish the scale and consequences of the problem. Add local evidence of the service gap, such as waitlists, referral records, or resident feedback. Distinguish the number of people affected from the number the project can serve.

**Phrasing hook:** “In [service area], [local finding] affects [population] ([source, year]). Existing services reach [group or volume] but leave [specific gap], which residents identified through [engagement method].”

### Approach — 1,000 words
**Include:** Start with a short explanation of why the proposed activities should address the gap. For each core activity, specify who delivers it, who receives it, where it happens, and how often. Show how participants enter and move through the program. Identify staff roles and time commitments, partner responsibilities, and milestones for startup, delivery, and follow-up.

**Phrasing hook:** “To address [barrier identified in Need], [staff role or partner] will deliver [activity] to [participants] at [frequency]. By [month or quarter], we will reach [implementation milestone].”

### Goals & Objectives — 425 words
**Include:** State the overall goal, then set two to four measurable objectives. Give each objective a population or denominator, a baseline or baseline collection point, a target, and a deadline. Label service counts as **outputs** and participant changes as **outcomes**. Don’t substitute zero for an unknown baseline.

**Phrasing hook:** “By [date], [X]% of [defined participant group] will achieve [threshold], compared with [baseline or intake measure]. Separately, [N] participants will complete [service].”

### Evaluation — 475 words
**Include:** For each objective, identify the indicator, tool or data source, collection schedule, and staff owner. Describe how you’ll handle incomplete follow-up and protect participant data. Explain when the team will review results and what decisions the findings will inform. If you’re using a pre/post design without a comparison group, describe observed change without claiming the program caused it.

**Phrasing hook:** “[Role] will collect [indicator] using [tool] at intake and [follow-up point]. The team will review [measure] quarterly and use the findings to adjust [specific program decision].”

### Sustainability — 150 words
**Include:** Name the activities that will continue after the grant, who will own them, and what resources they require. Distinguish secured support from funding you plan to pursue. If full continuation depends on new funding, identify what you can maintain with existing resources.

**Phrasing hook:** “After the grant ends, [team or partner] will maintain [core activity] using [confirmed resource]. Continuing [additional activity] at the proposed scale depends on [pending funding or decision].”

### Organizational Information — 150 words
**Include:** Give a one-sentence mission and service-area description, one comparable project with a documented result, and the operational capacity most relevant to this proposal. Keep project-specific staffing details in **Approach**.

**Phrasing hook:** “In [year], [Organization] delivered [comparable program] to [number and population] and achieved [documented result], demonstrating our ability to [relevant capability].”

### Budget Narrative — 400 words
**Include:** Use the same categories, order, and totals as the separately uploaded budget table. Explain the basis for major costs—such as salary × grant-funded staff time or unit cost × quantity—and link each to an activity. State the basis for any indirect costs or match. If cost per participant is useful, say whether it reflects the grant request or the full project cost, and whether the denominator is participants enrolled or served to completion.

**Phrasing hook:** “The $[amount] for [line item] covers [quantity] at $[rate] per [unit] and supports [activity]. The requested grant amount is $[cost] per [enrolled participant or completer], based on [N] projected [enrollees or completers].”

## Executive summary — about 200 words

[Organization] requests $[amount] for [Project Name], a [duration] initiative serving [number] [priority population] in [service area]. According to [source, year], [local statistic documenting the need]. [Community input or service data] identifies [specific barrier] as a gap in existing services. The project will address that gap by [brief explanation of how the program will help].

During the grant period, [staff roles] and [partners, if applicable] will deliver [activity 1], [activity 2], and [activity 3]. Participants will enter through [referral or outreach pathway] and receive [frequency or duration of services]. By [date], we expect [number] participants to complete [service] and [percentage] of [defined group] to achieve [measurable outcome]. We will establish or verify the baseline at [measurement point], track progress using [data source or tool], and review results [frequency] to guide program improvements.

The request will cover [major cost categories], at an estimated grant cost of $[amount] per [enrolled participant or completer]. [Organization] brings experience delivering [comparable program], which [documented result]. After the grant, we plan to sustain [core activity] through [confirmed resources or proposed funding strategy].

## Need

In 2023, 28% of adults in ZIP codes 12345–12347 had below-basic literacy, according to the Springfield County Department of Education’s *Adult Literacy Report 2023*.

These ZIP codes define the service area for the Literacy Boost Initiative in the Westside neighborhood of Springfield County. The local literacy rate establishes the scale of the problem: more than one in four adults in the service area had literacy skills below the report’s basic threshold. The figure measures literacy levels, not how many residents sought classes or needed a GED preparation program. Westside Learning Center’s enrollment records provide a separate measure of need: they show how many referrals led to enrollment, how many class slots the center offered, and how many people were waiting for a place.

The Literacy Boost Initiative will serve residents of ZIP codes 12345–12347 who are age 16 or older and have literacy skills at or below the eighth-grade level, as well as adults in those ZIP codes who are seeking a GED. These are two routes to eligibility. A resident seeking literacy instruction does not need to be pursuing a GED, and an adult seeking a GED does not need to meet the project’s literacy threshold. The county’s 28% figure describes below-basic literacy among adults; it does not count GED-seeking adults or establish the number of residents who meet the project’s full eligibility criteria.

Westside Learning Center’s records document a gap between referrals and enrollment. The center reported 210 referrals in 2024, of which 94 resulted in enrollment by December 31, 2024. About 45% of that year’s referrals led to enrollment by the reporting cutoff. The other 116 had not resulted in enrollment in the center’s records by that date. The records do not establish why each referral did not lead to enrollment, whether a resident enrolled elsewhere, or whether enrollment occurred after the cutoff. They do show that a referral to an existing service did not consistently translate into a class placement within the reporting period (Westside Learning Center, *Enrollment Reports 2024–2025*).

The center reported capacity for 40 class slots per quarter in 2024. At a September 30, 2025, snapshot, it had 86 individuals on its waitlist. The waitlist and capacity figures are from different periods, so they cannot establish the average wait or how quickly the center could have placed the people on the list. The 86 individuals also should not be added to the 116 referrals that had not led to enrollment: a person may appear in both records. What the waitlist does establish is that, after the 2024 reporting period, the center still had a documented queue of people waiting for service (Westside Learning Center, *Enrollment Reports 2024–2025*).

A resident described what that gap meant for their GED plans: “I want to finish my GED but classes are full for months.” The quote is one resident’s account, not a measure of typical wait times. It illustrates the difference between knowing where to seek GED preparation and being able to start a class. The center’s records establish that people were waiting for placement; the resident’s account shows how a wait can interrupt a specific education goal even when someone has already decided to pursue it.

The service gap is not the absence of a local provider. Westside Learning Center already offers classes and enrolls residents referred to it. The gap is access to a class placement. The county report documents the prevalence of below-basic literacy in the service area, while the center’s records document what happened among people who were referred or placed on a waitlist. Those sources answer different questions, but together they establish the case for increasing access: the underlying literacy need extends across the service area, and existing enrollment records show that not everyone who reached the local provider started a class by the reporting cutoff.

From January 1, 2027, through December 31, 2028, the Literacy Boost Initiative plans to serve 180 unique adults. The project will address the documented gap by adding opportunities for eligible residents to begin literacy instruction or GED preparation. The target of 180 is a count of distinct adults the project plans to serve. It is not a count of class slots, a forecast of completions, or an estimate of everyone in the three ZIP codes who needs instruction. The project’s intended contribution is to give more residents a place to start, alongside the services Westside Learning Center already provides.

The need this proposal addresses is specific: residents in the Westside service area need access to literacy instruction and GED preparation, and local records show that a referral alone has not reliably led to enrollment. The Literacy Boost Initiative will focus its grant-period resources on expanding access to instruction for eligible residents in ZIP codes 12345–12347. Its proposed reach is narrower than the community-wide need, but it responds directly to the barrier documented by the provider’s enrollment and waitlist records: getting a place in class.

Clarify how repeat participation, projected enrollment, or another planning assumption translates those slots into 180 distinct people, and whether eligible 16- and 17-year-olds count toward that target.
